# Open-Addressing Hash Table from Scratch

## Thesis

A hash table is a **dense array of slots** plus a hash that picks where to start looking. **Open addressing** stores every key in that array and resolves collisions by probing the next slot — no pointer-chasing buckets. The boring production rules are: pick a good hash, keep the load factor under ~0.7, resize by doubling, and never leave a "deleted" hole without a tombstone plan. This chapter builds a tiny C table with FNV-1a hashing and linear probing, then times 100 000 inserts.

## Mental model

```text
  key ──FNV-1a──► start index
                     │
                     ▼
              slots[i], slots[i+1], …   (linear probe)
                     │
          empty? → insert / stop lookup
          same key? → update
          other key? → keep probing
```

| Piece | Role |
|-------|------|
| `hash(key)` | Maps string → `uint64`; FNV-1a is short and good enough for teaching |
| `cap` | Power-of-two-ish size of the slot array (we double from 16) |
| `len / cap` | Load factor; grow before it crosses ~0.7 |
| Probe sequence | Here: `(h + i) % cap` for `i = 0,1,2…` |

## Worked examples

Verified with **gcc** `-O2` on Linux/amd64 (box kernel 6.12.94+).

### Case 1: FNV-1a + linear probe + grow

```c
// ht.c — open addressing with linear probe
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <time.h>

typedef struct { char *key; int value; int used; } Slot;
typedef struct { Slot *slots; size_t cap; size_t len; } HT;

static uint64_t hash(const char *s) {
  uint64_t h = 14695981039346656037ull;
  for (; *s; s++) { h ^= (unsigned char)*s; h *= 1099511628211ull; }
  return h;
}

static void ht_grow(HT *t);

static void ht_put(HT *t, const char *key, int value) {
  if ((t->len + 1) * 10 >= t->cap * 7) ht_grow(t);
  uint64_t h = hash(key);
  for (size_t i = 0; i < t->cap; i++) {
    size_t idx = (h + i) % t->cap;
    if (!t->slots[idx].used) {
      t->slots[idx].key = strdup(key);
      t->slots[idx].value = value;
      t->slots[idx].used = 1;
      t->len++;
      return;
    }
    if (strcmp(t->slots[idx].key, key) == 0) {
      t->slots[idx].value = value;
      return;
    }
  }
}

static void ht_grow(HT *t) {
  size_t ncap = t->cap ? t->cap * 2 : 16;
  Slot *old = t->slots; size_t ocap = t->cap;
  t->slots = calloc(ncap, sizeof(Slot));
  t->cap = ncap; t->len = 0;
  for (size_t i = 0; i < ocap; i++)
    if (old[i].used) { ht_put(t, old[i].key, old[i].value); free(old[i].key); }
  free(old);
}

static int ht_get(HT *t, const char *key, int *out) {
  uint64_t h = hash(key);
  for (size_t i = 0; i < t->cap; i++) {
    size_t idx = (h + i) % t->cap;
    if (!t->slots[idx].used) return 0;
    if (strcmp(t->slots[idx].key, key) == 0) { *out = t->slots[idx].value; return 1; }
  }
  return 0;
}

int main(void) {
  HT t = {0};
  char buf[32];
  struct timespec a, b;
  clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &a);
  for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "k%d", i);
    ht_put(&t, buf, i);
  }
  clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &b);
  double ms = (b.tv_sec - a.tv_sec) * 1e3 + (b.tv_nsec - a.tv_nsec) / 1e6;
  int v = 0; ht_get(&t, "k12345", &v);
  printf("inserted 100000 keys in %.2f ms; cap=%zu len=%zu; get k12345 -> %d\n",
         ms, t.cap, t.len, v);
  return 0;
}
```

```bash
cc -O2 -o ht ht.c && ./ht
```

Output from this run:

```
inserted 100000 keys in 31.74 ms; cap=262144 len=100000; get k12345 -> 12345
```

Load factor after the last grow: `100000 / 262144 ≈ 0.38` — we grew early because the check fires at 0.7 of the *previous* capacity.

## Trap

**Deleting without tombstones.** If you clear a slot to `used=0`, a later lookup that probed past it stops early and "loses" keys that live further along the probe chain. Either refuse deletes, or mark tombstones and treat them as "continue probing" on lookup while reusable on insert.

## Boring rule

Ship open addressing only with (1) a measured load-factor grow, (2) a documented delete story, and (3) a hash you did not invent on the day of the outage. For production C, prefer a reviewed library (SwissTable ports, `khash`, etc.) unless the table *is* the product.

## Try this

1. Switch linear probe to **quadratic** (`i*i`) and compare insert time at load 0.7.
2. Add tombstone deletes and a test that removes every even key then looks up every odd key.
3. Replace `strdup` with an arena so destroy is one free.
